name: Tara Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Tara, thanks for coming. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and your name won't be on anything. So you can tell me the version you'd say in the canteen and the version you'd only say to yourself.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. Fair warning, I've got opinions on this, because AI already took one job off me. So I'm not exactly neutral, but I'm not angry either.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start with today. What's a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee carpenter with one of the big contractors on the new hospital extension. Right now I'm on temporary works, building the timber hoarding round the site, the walkways, the edge protection, and some first-fix stud walls inside. I came in at forty after fifteen years on the phones at an insurance call centre, which got replaced by chatbots almost overnight. I use AI all day, honestly, I photograph the drawings and get it to explain them, and I use it to translate for Andrei and Mihai, who are brilliant carpenters but whose English is still coming along. What wears me out is the early starts and being the slowest one with a saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a good helper and it stopped there. Though I'd also say it didn't feel like hype when it took my last job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief, and a bit funny. I'd have jumped out of an office into construction to escape something that then didn't come any further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the hospital job, finish my trade certificate, and carry on using AI to learn faster than I would otherwise. Maybe offer to show the supervisors how to use it to sort out their paperwork, because that gets you noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bit of an eye-roll at all the fuss, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the call centre.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fifteen years answering calls about car insurance claims. Then in one year they brought in a chatbot that handled most of it, and three hundred of us became forty. I saw it coming about six months before, and I was one of the first to leave, which is the only reason I got into a training scheme here before everyone else tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is money at home right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thin. Marco drives the number twelve bus, and between us we just about cover the mortgage and the kids. We've got maybe two or three weeks of money if anything went wrong, and last year when the car failed its test we had to borrow from his sister.

S0.say: Fair enough, it's a good helper and it stopped there. But I'd also say it didn't feel like hype when it took my last job.
S0.think: It'd be a relief, and a bit funny. I jumped out of an office into construction to escape something that then didn't come any further.
S0.do: Keeps working on the hospital extension and finishes her trade certificate, using AI to learn faster. Offers to show supervisors how AI can handle their paperwork, to get herself noticed.
S0.feel: Calm, with a bit of an eye-roll at all the fuss.
S0.quote: Then in one year they brought in a chatbot that handled most of it, and three hundred of us became forty.
S0.fieldNote: She has already been through one AI-driven job loss and survived it by moving early. That experience makes her watchful rather than bitter. She uses AI to bridge language gaps on site and to make up for her lack of experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ahead of it, don't wait to be pushed. That's what I tell anyone who'll listen. And I'd say employers should pay for the training, because they get the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do okay. I've already moved once and I'm not scared of new tech. I'd want to be the person on site who runs the new machines, not the one standing next to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As soon as the contractor brings in anything new, layout robots, drones for surveying, I'd ask to be trained on it. I'd do online courses at night about site technology, and I'd keep using AI every day to get better at reading plans. If my contractor won't train me, I'd look at the ones that will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Even a bit excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be looking out for on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who's buying what kit, which supervisors are curious and which ones are digging in. Last month a little robot came on site that draws the wall lines on the floor from the drawings, and I spent my lunch watching the engineer use it. I asked him about fifteen questions and he gave me his number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That worries me more than my job. They're already testing buses that drive themselves on the airport route. He's fifty-one and he's been driving for twenty years, and he hates computers, he won't even use the bank app.

S1.say: Get ahead of it, don't wait to be pushed. And employers should pay for the training, because they're the ones getting the savings.
S1.think: I think I'd do okay, since I've already moved once and I'm not scared of new tech. I want to be the person on site who runs the new machines, not the one standing next to them.
S1.do: Asks to be trained on any new kit such as layout robots or survey drones as soon as her contractor brings it in. Takes online courses on site technology at night and looks for another contractor if hers won't train her.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, even a little excited.
S1.quote: I spent my lunch watching the engineer use it. I asked him about fifteen questions and he gave me his number.
S1.fieldNote: She already treats new site technology as her way up, and has been actively seeking it out. Her calm about her own job sits next to real worry about her partner, an older bus driver who avoids technology. She expects employers to pay for training but is ready to move firms if they won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone needs to move now, today, and the government needs to put money into helping people through it. I'd be posting practical stuff, which courses, which firms are hiring, because that's more useful than shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's frightening. If AI can do almost any job, then being quick doesn't help so much, there's less to jump to. And Marco and I could both lose our jobs in the same year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase any job connected to setting up and running the robots, even if it means a longer commute or nights. I'd start doing small jobs for cash on weekends, hanging doors, flat-pack furniture, while people still pay a person. And I'd cut back hard at home straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit angry with myself, because I thought I'd found the safe place. Like I ran from the flood and it followed me up the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've moved early once before. Would two years be enough to do it again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last time I had six months of warning and I used every week of it. Two years for everything to change, for everyone at once, is different. When everyone's jumping at the same time, there are a lot more people at the same door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The streaming services, the takeaways, Nina's swimming lessons, sadly. Then the car, if Marco can get to the depot by bike. The mortgage is the last thing we'd let go.

S2.say: Everyone needs to move now, today, and the government needs to put money into helping people through it. I'd post practical stuff, which courses and which firms are hiring, because that's more useful than shouting.
S2.think: It's frightening, because if AI can do almost any job, there's less to jump to. And Marco and I could both lose our jobs in the same year.
S2.do: Chases any job setting up or running robots, even with a longer commute or night shifts, and does weekend handyman jobs for cash. Cuts streaming, takeaways, swimming lessons and possibly the car.
S2.feel: Scared and angry with herself for thinking she'd found a safe place, as if the flood followed her up the hill.
S2.quote: Like I ran from the flood and it followed me up the hill.
S2.fieldNote: Her past success at moving early gives her less comfort here, because everyone would be jumping at once. She still reaches for practical action and useful information rather than complaint. Both household incomes being exposed is what tips her from confident to alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a head start, so use it. Learn the new kit, change if you have to, and push employers to train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a good amount for me. I could get from trainee carpenter to someone who sets up and checks the machines, if I'm smart about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask my contractor to put me on the robot layout and drone survey courses, and I'd keep learning every evening online. I'd save whatever I could, maybe sixty a month. I'd also try to help Marco start learning something new, slowly, because he'll need time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like before an exam you've actually studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that their mum got replaced by a computer once and then learned to build hospitals, and that I'm going to learn something new again. I want them to see that you can change. And I'd tell Leo to keep doing the things he loves, he's great with people, and that's going to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Nina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, mostly. I'd sit with him in the evenings and go through the courses together, the way I helped my mum with her phone. He'd grumble, but he'd do it for the kids.

S3.say: Five years is a head start, so use it. Learn the new kit, change if you have to, and push employers to train people.
S3.think: Five years is a good amount for me. I could get from trainee carpenter to someone who sets up and checks the machines, if I'm smart about it.
S3.do: Asks her contractor this year for places on robot layout and drone survey courses and keeps studying online every evening. Saves about 60 a month and helps her partner Marco start learning new skills slowly.
S3.feel: Anxious in a busy way, like before an exam she has studied for.
S3.quote: I'd tell them that their mum got replaced by a computer once and then learned to build hospitals, and that I'm going to learn something new again.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she has a clear route from trainee carpenter to machine setup and checking. Much of her plan is about bringing her partner along, which shows she sees the household as one unit. She wants her children to see change as something you can survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, with proper training and planning. No excuses, for governments or companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years feels quite good for me. I'd be fifty-three, I'd have time to get really good at the new kind of work, and the kids would be grown up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, finish my trade and get onto every bit of new kit the contractor brings in. Then move into machine setup or site technology work properly, maybe with a different firm. I'd save what I could and help the kids pick paths that make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than worried. It feels like something I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years change compared with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I could actually plan, instead of grabbing whatever's going. I could do a proper course, not just the quick ones, and make sure Marco gets something set up before his driving goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything about your kids' plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Leo's twelve, so in ten years he's choosing what to do. I'd push him towards jobs where you look after people or fix the machines, not ones a computer can do from a desk, because I did fifteen years of one of those and I know how fast they can go.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this well, with proper training and planning. No excuses for governments or companies.
S4.think: Ten years feels quite good for me. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown up, and I'd have time to get really good at the new kind of work.
S4.do: Finishes her trade and learns every new piece of kit her contractor brings in over the first few years. Then moves into machine setup or site technology work, saves what she can, and steers her children's career choices.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more interested than worried, because she can plan for it.
S4.quote: I did fifteen years of one of those and I know how fast they can go.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her plan properly rather than grab whatever is going, and she relaxes noticeably. Her worry shifts to her son's career choice, shaped by her own call centre past. Her focus on her partner's driving job runs through every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because when everyone's jumping at once, being quick isn't enough, and Marco would be in trouble too. What would help is employers paying for real training on the new machines, and some money to keep families going while they switch. Being told which jobs will actually exist would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who've already been replaced once. We know what it's like, and we know what helped and what didn't. The leaflets didn't help, the training scheme that paid me while I learned did.

headlineQuote: The leaflets didn't help, the training scheme that paid me while I learned did.
portrait: Tara is a 43-year-old trainee carpenter on a hospital extension for a big contractor, who moved into building after chatbots replaced most of her insurance call centre. She uses AI every day to read drawings and translate for colleagues, and seeks out new site technology. She is calm in the plateau and steady pictures, alarmed by AGI in two years because she and her bus driver partner could both lose work while everyone jumps at once, and steadier with five or ten years to plan. She wants employers to pay for training, and much of her planning is about helping her partner and children through the change.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because being quick isn't enough when everyone is jumping at once, and her partner Marco would be in trouble too.
whatWouldHelp: Employers paying for real training on new machines, money to keep families going during the switch, and clear information on which jobs will exist.
